questions.q: State the fundamental difference between sampling error and non-sampling error that determines whether increasing the sample size can reduce the error.
questions.a: Sampling error arises solely from using a subset (sample) instead of the whole population and decreases as sample size increases; non-sampling error arises from flaws in the data collection process (measurement, recording, coverage, non-response) and persists even in a complete census, so increasing sample size does not reduce it. A wrong answer (e.g., "both decrease with larger samples") reveals the student has not grasped that non-sampling errors are systematic process errors, not random sampling variability.

questions.q: A researcher wants to estimate the average yield of wheat per hectare in Punjab. She selects 100 farms using simple random sampling. During the survey, 15 farmers refuse to participate, 5 enumerators consistently record yield in quintals instead of kg, and the sampling frame excludes tenant farmers who cultivate leased land. Classify each issue as sampling bias, non-response error, or data acquisition error.
questions.a: Excluding tenant farmers from the sampling frame = sampling bias (some population members have zero chance of selection). 15 farmers refusing = non-response error (sample observations missing, may not be representative). Enumerators recording in wrong units = data acquisition error (incorrect recording/measurement). A wrong classification (e.g., calling unit error "sampling bias") reveals confusion between error sources: sampling bias is about WHO is selected, non-response is about WHO responds, data acquisition is about HOW data is recorded.

questions.q: In a national health survey, the questionnaire asks: "How many times did you visit a doctor in the last year?" Respondents tend to round their answers to the nearest 5 (e.g., saying 10 instead of 8). The survey uses a sample of 50,000 households. If the sample size is doubled to 100,000, will the rounding error decrease? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: No, the rounding error will not decrease. Rounding is a data acquisition error (measurement error) caused by respondent memory limitations and questionnaire design — it is systematic and affects every respondent similarly regardless of sample size. Doubling the sample only reduces sampling error (random variability), not this systematic bias. A student who answers "yes" misunderstands that non-sampling errors are properties of the measurement process, not sample size.

questions.q: Compare the impact of non-sampling errors in a census versus a sample survey of the same population. Which is more vulnerable to non-sampling errors and why? Consider both the magnitude of error and the ability to detect it.
questions.a: A census is MORE vulnerable to non-sampling errors in absolute terms because: (1) it involves more enumerators, increasing inconsistency in measurement and recording; (2) supervision and training quality dilute with larger field force; (3) data processing volume increases entry/tabulation errors; (4) non-response is harder to follow up at scale. However, a sample survey's estimates may be MORE biased if non-sampling errors correlate with the sampling design (e.g., non-response concentrated in certain strata). The key insight: census eliminates sampling error but amplifies non-sampling error sources — this is why NSSO uses sample surveys despite having census capability.

questions.q: A student argues: "Since non-sampling errors cannot be reduced by increasing sample size, we should always use a census to avoid sampling error entirely." Evaluate this argument using the concepts of total survey error and resource constraints.
questions.a: The argument is flawed because: (1) Total Survey Error = Sampling Error + Non-Sampling Error. A census sets sampling error to zero but typically increases non-sampling error due to larger operational scale (more enumerators, less supervision per unit, greater processing burden). (2) With fixed resources, a well-designed sample survey with intensive training, supervision, and follow-up can yield lower TOTAL error than a poorly executed census. (3) Timeliness: census takes years; sample gives timely data for policy. The student ignores the trade-off between error types and resource allocation — a classic board exam trap.

questions.q: Design a 4-question mini-questionnaire to collect data on "monthly household expenditure on vegetables" that MINIMIZES all three types of non-sampling errors. For each question, explain which error type it addresses and how.
questions.a:
Good answer includes:
Q1: "Does your household purchase vegetables regularly? (Yes/No)" — screens eligibility, reduces coverage error (sampling bias) by identifying in-scope units.
Q2: "In the last 30 days, how much did your household spend on vegetables? (Record exact amount in rupees: ₹____)" — uses reference period and exact amount, reduces recall error and rounding (data acquisition error).
Q3: "Who in the household usually purchases vegetables? (Name: ____)" — identifies best respondent, reduces proxy-response error (data acquisition).
Q4: "May we verify this with your purchase receipts or digital payment history? (Yes/No)" — enables validation, reduces recording error and social desirability bias (data acquisition/non-response).
Each question targets a specific error mechanism. A poor answer lists generic questions without linking to error types.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Non-sampling errors are systematic deviations of survey estimates from true population values that arise from flaws in data collection, recording, processing, or analysis, rather than from the random ______ inherent in using a sample instead of a census.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you conduct a census of all 500 households in a village to find average monthly ______ on education.
What is Non-sampling errors? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Non-sampling errors are systematic deviations of survey estimates from true population values that arise from flaws in data collection, recording, processing, or analysis, rather than from the random variability inherent in using a sample instead of a census.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: You hire ______ enumerators, give them a questionnaire, and collect data from every single household.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Non-sampling errors?
questions.a: Students often confuse "sampling bias" (a non-sampling error) with "sampling error" because both contain the word "sampling." They think sampling bias is a type of sampling error that can be fixed by larger samples.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) distinguish non-sampling errors from sampling errors using the defining characteristic of persistence in census, (2) classify a given real-world data collection scenario into the three NCERT categories (sampling bias, non-response error, data acquisition error), and (3) explain why increasing sample size.
